payload.title: Counting Birds from the Kitchen Window
paragraphs: Every January, close to half a million people in Britain spend one hour watching the birds in their gardens and send the results to a conservation charity. The instructions are deliberately simple: count the highest number of each species you see at any one time, not the total number of visits, and record nothing you merely heard. The scheme has run since 1979, which makes it one of the longest continuous surveys of wildlife anywhere.

Its value lies less in any single year than in the trend. Individual counts are noisy, because a cold snap or a neighbour's new cat can empty a garden for a morning. Spread across hundreds of thousands of gardens, however, those accidents cancel out, and slow changes become visible that no team of professionals could afford to measure. The decline of the house sparrow, now down by more than half since the survey began, was first noticed in exactly this way.

The organisers are honest about what the data cannot show. Gardens are not the countryside, and species that avoid people are missed entirely. Participants are also more likely to live in suburbs than on farms, so the map of sightings is partly a map of who took part. Even so, the charity argues that an imperfect record kept for fifty years is worth more than a perfect one that nobody can afford to keep.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: A long-running volunteer bird count is unreliable in any single garden or year, but across huge numbers of gardens it reveals trends that professionals could never afford to track, despite known gaps in what it records.
Professional scientists have rejected the survey because the counting method ignores birds that are heard but not seen.
The survey's main achievement has been to reverse the decline of the house sparrow in British gardens since 1979.
Because most participants live in suburbs, the charity has decided to restrict future counts to farms and open countryside.

questions.after: by chance events such as bad weather, the organisers rely on the combined results of many thousands of participants.

payload.title: A Bus That Comes When You Call
paragraphs: In the hills north of the town, the number 32 bus used to run four times a day along a fixed route, and on most trips it carried fewer than three passengers. Last spring the council replaced it with something different. There is no timetable and no set route; instead, residents book a seat through an app or a phone line, and a small minibus plans its journey around the requests it receives.

The early results surprised even the people who designed the scheme. Passenger numbers have more than doubled, partly because the minibus now stops close to people's homes rather than at a distant shelter on the main road. Older residents, who were expected to struggle with the app, have become its most regular users, usually by phoning a coordinator who books for them.

Not everyone is pleased. Some people miss the certainty of a printed timetable and dislike having to plan a trip the evening before. The council also admits that the service is more expensive to run per passenger than a conventional bus would be in a busy town. For a scattered rural population, though, it argues that the comparison is unfair: the real alternative was no bus at all.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: A rural council replaced an almost empty fixed-route bus with a bookable minibus, which has attracted far more passengers despite some complaints and a higher cost per rider.
The council cancelled the number 32 bus and now expects residents to rely on taxis and private cars.
Older residents refused to use the new service because it can only be booked through a smartphone app.
The new minibus follows the same route as the old bus but runs more often, which explains the rise in passengers.

questions.after: because the only realistic alternative in the area was no service at all.
